findings.paper_title: Annex B - Performance and Resources Report – Q4 2025/26
findings.headline: Allowance for doubtful debts increased significantly to £17.7m, driven by legacy adult social care contributions
findings.detail: The allowance for doubtful debtors was increased by £5.482m in 2025/26 to reach £17.7m. A significant proportion of aged debt relates to historic adult social care contributions, reflecting legacy impacts from COVID-19, delays in assessment processes, and ongoing economic pressures. The council notes strengthened controls are now in place but the problem is substantial.
findings.matters: A large doubtful debt provision is both an immediate hit to resources and a signal of underlying income collection problems. The link to social care assessments and COVID-19 legacy suggests structural delays in the council's processes.
findings.figures: Doubtful debt provision increased by £5.482m; total provision £17.7m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Recognising the risks associated with ageing debt, the Allowance for Doubtful Debtors has been increased with an additional £5.482m set aside. This brings the total Doubtful Debt provision to £17.7m as at 31 March 2026, ensuring a prudent and robust approach to financial risk management.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - Performance and Resources Report – Q4 2025/26
findings.headline: 39% of planned savings were not delivered in 2025/26 and are being pushed into 2026/27
findings.detail: Of the total £20.580m savings target for 2025/26 (including £8.327m reprofiled from prior years), only £12.489m (61%) were achieved. The £8.091m shortfall (39%) was undelivered and is expected to be delivered in full in 2026/27. Adults Services has £5.392m in red-rated savings with significant risk of non-delivery.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver planned savings, especially in the year they are due, indicates either operational challenges or optimistic planning. Pushing these into the next year while new pressures continue to emerge raises the risk of compounding deficits.
findings.figures: £20.580m total savings target; £12.489m delivered (61%); £8.091m unachieved (39%); Adults Services £5.392m at significant risk of non-delivery
findings.quote: Of the total £20.580m saving, £12.489m (61%) were achieved as originally envisaged or through a different way and £8.091m (39%) of savings were undelivered this year. These unachieved savings are included within the outturn position and are expected to be delivered in full in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - Performance and Resources Report – Q4 2025/26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £202.995m and represents the largest structural fiscal risk
findings.detail: The DSG deficit entered 2025/26 at £123.206m and grew by £79.741m in-year overspend to reach £202.995m. This is primarily driven by high needs blocks for independent and specialist placements. While the government announced a High Needs Stability Grant potentially covering 90% (approximately £182.7m for West Sussex), payment is contingent on the council's Local SEND Reform Plan being approved by the Department for Education.
findings.matters: A £203m deficit is a material contingent liability that affects the council's balance sheet and borrowing capacity. The grant cover is not guaranteed—approval of the SEND plan is a condition precedent. If not approved, the council's liability explodes.
findings.figures: DSG deficit increased to £202.995m (from £123.206m opening); potential grant cover approximately £182.7m (subject to approval)
findings.quote: The DSG Reserve entered the 2025/26 financial year with a deficit of £123.206m. After accounting for the in-year DSG overspend of £79.741m, and a minor adjustment of £0.048m to the Early Years block following DfE 2024/25 data reconciliation adjustment, the deficit on the DSG Unusable Reserve has increased to £202.995m.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - Performance and Resources Report – Q4 2025/26
findings.headline: Council overspent by £12.976m and drew down reserves to balance the budget
findings.detail: The council's provisional outturn shows a net overspend of £12.976m after using its contingency budget. To cover this, the council drew £6.0m from the Social Care Reserve (its intended purpose) and £6.976m from the Budget Management Reserve. This is a material drawdown of general-purpose reserves in a single year.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion signals the council is unable to absorb pressures from normal operations and is eating into its financial buffer. Repeated drawdowns in future years would eliminate resilience.
findings.figures: £12.976m net overspend; £6.0m from Social Care Reserve + £6.976m from Budget Management Reserve
findings.quote: the net £12.976m overspend has resulted in a required drawdown from reserves. As reported in previous PRR reports this year, the planned approach is to utilise £6.0m from the Social Care Reserve, reflecting its intended use to support social care overspending in 2025/26, with the remaining £6.976m to be drawn from the Budget Management Reserve.

findings.headline: Social care provider market instability presents material cost risk despite recent score improvement
findings.detail: The council depends on external care providers for social care delivery. The risk of large-scale provider failure or closure, driven by legislative changes, inflation, and National Living Wage pressures, is scored at current 15 (down from initial 25). Contingency plans for strategic and prime provider failure are due 01/08/2026. Fee review and market intelligence gathering are ongoing but the baseline risk remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Provider failure in social care directly translates to emergency cost absorption by the council or service cessation. The council explicitly notes 'significant increase in costs' as an outcome of provider instability.
findings.figures: Initial Score 25, Current Score 15, Target Score 8
findings.quote: There is a risk of large scale provider failure or failure of strategic or business critical services as a result of this instability which could result in significant increase in costs and residents of West Sussex being left without care.

findings.headline: Unplanned transfer of NHS Integrated Care Board functions without additional resource is an identified governance and financial risk
findings.detail: Following NHS England abolition and Surrey-Sussex ICB merger with reduced staffing, there is active risk that non-core ICB functions will be transferred to the council without agreement, governance clarity, legislation, timing certainty, or additional financial or operational resource. A mapping exercise of NHS organisational engagement is due 01/08/2026 to assess current gaps.
findings.matters: Unresourced function transfers would represent a sudden cost/capacity commitment with no associated funding, adding directly to the council's already-worsening financial sustainability position.
findings.figures: Risk raised 01/07/2025; mapping exercise due 01/08/2026; Initial/Current/Target scores: 16/16/6
findings.quote: There is a risk that the current ICB functions not considered to be core to strategic commissioning will be transferred to the council without agreement, governance (e.g. legislation, timing) or additional financial/operational resource.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability risk has escalated significantly, now above starting score and above target
findings.detail: The council's financial sustainability is scored at current 25 (up from initial 16, target 12), reflecting worsening pressures. The council identifies insufficient central government funding, inflation and interest rate impacts, and growing service pressures—particularly in social care, home to school transport and SEND—as the drivers. Risk controls consist of annual MTFS reviews, reserve monitoring, and lobbying for funding, with no structural solutions articulated.
findings.matters: An escalating financial risk score signals deteriorating financial position relative to the council's own assessment. Specific unresolved pressures in social care and SEND are material cost drivers that a lender would scrutinise.
findings.figures: Initial Score 16, Current Score 25, Target Score 12
findings.quote: The financial sustainability of council services is at risk due to the lack of new funding from central government, the impact of economic conditions (mainly inflation and interest rates) and the growing services pressures, particularly around social care, home to school transport and SEND.

findings.headline: Total useable reserves declining and being used unsustainably to cover annual budget gaps
findings.detail: Total Useable Reserves stood at £199.3m as of 31 March 2025 and are in declining trend. The council used £3.6m from reserves in 2024/25 to manage the budget deficit and is projected to continue drawing down reserves annually. The auditor explicitly notes that this pattern is 'not sustainable in the medium to long term'.
findings.matters: Reliance on reserves to plug annual deficits is inherently temporary and leaves the council vulnerable if budget pressures worsen, Council Tax income falls short, or if the DSG deficit materialises earlier than expected

findings.quote: Although the Council has a healthy level of reserves, the use of reserves in not sustainable in the medium to long term. Continued use of these reserves to balance the budget will continue to erode these reserves.

findings.detail: Portfolio budgets exceeded spending limits by £32.9m, with total net revenue expenditure reaching £828.5m against a budget of £795.6m. The overspend was primarily in the Children and Young People and Adult Services portfolios, only partially offset by non-portfolio underspends. This pattern reflects acknowledged service delivery pressures that the council expects to persist.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that demand-led services are materially overrunning budget and that the council itself acknowledges these pressures are expected to continue, suggesting budget control challenges

findings.headline: Cumulative budget deficit of £203.9m over five years with structural reliance on Council Tax rises and reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The October 2024 Medium Term Financial Plan shows annual budget gaps from 2025/26 onwards with a cumulative deficit of £203.9m by March 2030. Even assuming maximum Council Tax increases of £30.3m to £38.1m annually plus budget reductions of £8.6m and £4.5m in the first two years, a £33.4m cumulative shortfall remains. The plan explicitly states the council will need to identify further savings and additional funding sources to sustain its financial position.
findings.matters: The council faces a structural funding gap that cannot be closed by existing savings plans, making the financial position unsustainable without either further council tax rises above planned levels or additional government funding
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £203.9m by March 2030; Council Tax increases £30.3m-£38.1m p.a.; budget reductions £8.6m (2025/26), £4.5m (2026/27); residual gap £33.4m
findings.quote: This highlighted a budget gap each year from 2025/26, and a cumulative deficit after savings of £203.9 million at 31 March 2030. The Council will need to identify further savings and additional funding sources in order to sustain their financial position.

findings.detail: The DSG deficit has grown from £71.6m in March 2024 to £123.2m in March 2025 and is forecast to reach £223m by March 2026. The council is particularly concerned about its ability to fund this deficit when temporary legislation allowing it to sit outside the General Fund expires in March 2028, as the deficit will then exceed the combined General Fund and Other Useable Reserves.
findings.matters: A lender would view this as a significant financial sustainability risk: a £223m deficit that will become immediately problematic when the legislative reprieve expires in 2028, requiring either emergency funding or service cuts

findings.quote: The current deficit is forecast to increase in coming periods and will be greater than the sum of the Councils General Fund and Other Useable Reserves combined. It is also reducing money available to be invested short term and generate investment income.

findings.detail: Capital financing costs (debt service) rise from £32.2m in 2025/26 to £57.4m by 2030/31. As a proportion of net revenue expenditure, this grows from 3.8% to 5.5%, representing an increasing claim on the revenue budget by servicing the capital programme.
findings.matters: Rising debt service ratios indicate a growing proportion of the revenue budget is locked into financing past and current borrowing, potentially constraining the council's ability to invest in service delivery.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Costs: 2025/26 £32.2m (3.8% of revenue); 2030/31 £57.4m (5.5% of revenue)

findings.headline: Internal borrowing buffer of £77m erodes to zero by 2027/28, eliminating financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council currently holds £77.4m in underborrowing (11.8% of CFR), representing internal resources available to offset external borrowing if needed. This buffer declines sharply to zero by 2027/28 and remains at zero thereafter, indicating the council will have no internal financial reserves to manage unexpected pressures from that point forward.
findings.matters: The loss of this buffer indicates the council is moving to full external financing and signals reduced capacity to absorb financial shocks without accessing the market.
findings.quote: Under/Over(-) Borrowing as a % of CFR 11.8% 19.2% 4.4% 0.0% 0.0% 0.0% 0.0%

findings.headline: External debt forecast to grow 69% over six years, from £444m to £749m
findings.detail: Gross external debt is projected to increase from £444.2m in 2025/26 to £748.7m by 2030/31. This growth reflects both a rising capital financing requirement (from £677.8m to £960.6m) and increasing PFI and finance lease liabilities, representing a material expansion of the council's debt stock.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the trajectory and scale of a council's borrowing commitments. A 69% increase in external debt over six years signals significant capital ambition and future servicing obligations.
findings.figures: Gross External Debt: 2025/26 £444.2m; 2030/31 £748.7m. Capital Financing Requirement (Closing Balance): 2025/26 £677.8m; 2030/31 £960.6m

findings.paper_title: Annex 2a - Appendix A: Capital Programme 2026/27 and 2030/31
findings.headline: 2027/28 capital expenditure peaks at £195.4m—a 37% spike above 2026/27, creating delivery and financing risk
findings.detail: The 2027/28 year shows unusually concentrated spending of £195.4m (compared to £142.3m in 2026/27), driven primarily by children's services (£54.1m) and highways (£71.2m). This concentration creates project delivery risk and financing stress in a single year.
findings.matters: A high-peak-year capital programme is harder to execute and finance smoothly. If delivery slips or costs overrun in 2027/28, the council lacks headroom to absorb the impact without cascading into the following year.
findings.figures: 2027/28 total £195,431k vs 2026/27 £142,323k (37% increase); Children's Young People and Learning 2027/28 £54,078k; Highways and Transport 2027/28 £71,173k

findings.headline: Highway improvement programme front-loaded with uncertain grant continuation beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: Highways and Transport programme totals £308.3m. 2026/27 is heavily grant-funded (Department for Transport grants £11.8m, Local Transport Grant £4m, Bus Service Improvement Plan £6.1m), but grant funding drops sharply or ends in later years, forcing the council to fund future years primarily from borrowing. The A259 Bognor to Littlehampton scheme (£40.8m total) shows external grant dependency but corporate resources fill most gaps.
findings.matters: Grant-dependent programmes are vulnerable to government policy change. When this grant funding ends, the council will need to either cancel schemes or fund them from borrowing, reducing financial flexibility.

findings.headline: Children's services showing substantial unfinanced expansion beyond existing commitments
findings.detail: Proposed starts in children's services total £122m over 5 years, dominated by Future Years Basic Need (£65.5m) and school maintenance/sufficiency programmes. These are on top of £94.6m already in-flight, creating a £216.7m total programme. The front-loading to 2027/28 (£54.1m) suggests a peak delivery year driven by demographic pressures or sufficiency concerns not explained in this document.
findings.matters: Education sufficiency costs are structural, not discretionary. This signals either population growth the council is planning for, or an existing shortfall it must remedy. Either way, it drives long-term borrowing and revenue budget pressure.
findings.figures: Children, Young People and Learning total programme £216,686k; Future Years Basic Need £65,479k; 2027/28 peak £54,078k

findings.paper_title: Annex 2a - Appendix A: Capital Programme 2026/27 and 2030/31
findings.headline: Borrowing finances over half the capital programme, replacing rapidly declining capital receipts
findings.detail: £442.2m of the £842.1m programme (52.5%) is funded by borrowing: £354.1m core borrowing and £88.1m economic development borrowing. Capital receipts have collapsed from £12m (2025/26) to £4.3m (2026/27) and decline further each year, shifting the financing burden entirely to borrowing and reducing the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can service £442m of additional borrowing while capital receipts—the primary internal funding source—are drying up. This indicates structural reliance on external borrowing to fund the capital programme.
findings.figures: Core Borrowing £354,065k; Economic Development Borrowing £88,148k; Capital Receipts declining from £12,000k to £4,300k

findings.headline: Recruitment and retention challenges in social workers, care workers, and planners, worsened by LGR transition
findings.detail: The council faces ongoing difficulty recruiting and retaining social workers, care workers, occupational therapists, planners, and lawyers. Document notes these 'areas of pressure' will be compounded by the structural uncertainty of local government reorganisation between 2026 and 2028.
findings.matters: Unfilled posts in social care drive agency spending and service delays. During a period of service demand pressure and budget cuts, recruitment challenges create delivery risk.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: The County Council continues to face recruitment and retention challenges in some areas with Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation likely to add further challenge. Whilst improved, areas of pressure continue to be social workers, care workers and occupational therapists, planners, property, transport and development professionals and lawyers.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation by April 2028 creates uncertainty during financial stress period; transformation roadmap not yet set
findings.detail: County Council must merge with district and borough councils by April 2028, but Government has not yet decided the configuration. A single unitary council would deliver £30m/year efficiency savings but would take 2.3 years to break even. The council's transformation programme will be 'reviewed once a decision on local government reorganisation is confirmed,' meaning current plans may need to change.
findings.matters: Structural change to financing and service delivery during period of greatest financial stress; transformation costs and benefits are contingent on a decision not yet made by Government.
findings.figures: £30m/year savings (single unitary); 2.3 years to break even; £5.9m transformation savings in 2026/27
findings.quote: The business case shows that a single unitary offers greater resilience, increased capacity, and delivers significantly higher efficiency savings (£48 million annually compared to £18.8 million for a two unitary authority). Additionally, transformation costs would be recovered in less than half the time (2.3 years for a one unitary authority versus 6.3 years for two).

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit costs £8.3m in lost investment income in 2026/27 despite statutory override
findings.detail: Although the DSG deficit is protected from the balance sheet by statutory override until March 2028, the unresolved deficit still creates a cash impact through lost investment returns. Government support for historic DSG deficits remains undefined and 'any future support will not be unlimited.'
findings.matters: Ongoing financial drag from unresolved SEND system failure. Historic deficits are undefined and create future funding uncertainty that could require additional budget support.
findings.figures: £8.3m lost investment income in 2026/27; statutory override extends to March 2028
findings.quote: the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit which, although it is not part of the County Council's balance sheet because of the statutory over-ride in place until 2028, is resulting in lost investment income of an estimated £8.3m in 2026/27

findings.headline: Budget balance entirely dependent on maximum 4.99% council tax rise; no revenue flexibility
findings.detail: The council can only achieve Core Spending Power growth by applying the full 4.99% council tax increase. Of the £40m CSP increase for 2026/27, 'all of this increase is attributable to the council tax assumptions and not increased government funding.' The council explicitly warns that not taking the full rise would lose funding Government assumes is available.
findings.matters: Zero revenue flexibility; the council is politically and financially locked into maximum tax rises to avoid service cuts. This removes any buffer if tax base falls short or allowable increase is capped.
findings.figures: £40m CSP increase entirely from council tax; 4.99% rise assumed in MTFS
findings.quote: Not increasing Council Tax by the full 4.99% would mean the County Council would lose out on funding the Government assumes is available to us to deal with pressures.

findings.headline: Adults and Children's Social Care demand is driving current and forecast overspend
findings.detail: The £19.7m current-year overspend is 'largely driven by the demand and complexities in both Adults and Children's Social Care.' The council also calls out ongoing demand pressures on home-to-school transport. These are statutory services with limited levers for cost control.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled demand in mandatory services limits management flexibility and creates cumulative budget risk. The council has no discretion to reduce these services.
findings.figures: £19.7m overspend attributed to social care; service demand cited as ongoing risk
findings.quote: The forecasted overspend position for 2025/26 is largely driven by the demand and complexities in both Adults and Children's Social Care.

findings.headline: £30.4m efficiency savings required to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council must deliver £30.4m of operational efficiency savings to balance its 2026/27 budget alongside the maximum council tax rise. These savings sit alongside simultaneous transformation programmes with uncertain delivery timelines.
findings.matters: Savings delivery risk is material; if these targets are missed, the budget fails. The council is simultaneously running LGR transition and Connected Council transformation, which creates delivery risk.
findings.figures: £30.4m efficiency savings required; £5.9m from transformation programmes accelerated into 2026/27
findings.quote: balancing the budget for 2026/27 is only possible by introducing the Government's presumed 4.99% increase in Council Tax and efficiency savings across services of £30.4m

findings.headline: £72.5m budget gap forecast between 2026/27 and 2030/31 even with maximum council tax increases
findings.detail: The medium-term financial strategy shows a structural deficit of £72.5m over the five-year period, assuming the council takes the maximum 4.99% council tax rise every year. This gap signals future service reductions or further revenue measures.
findings.matters: A £72.5m structural gap signals the council's current operating model is not sustainable; it will require either significant service reductions or revenue measures beyond current council tax maximums.
findings.quote: budget gap of £72.5m between 2026/27 and 2030/31 assuming a full 4.99% Council Tax increase in these years

findings.headline: September 2025 forecast shows £19.7m revenue overspend in 2025/26, exceeding the £10m contingency buffer
findings.detail: Current-year outturn is forecast to exceed contingency, requiring reserve drawdown. The council notes this will mark the third consecutive year of relying on one-off funding to balance the budget, which it explicitly describes as 'not financially sustainable in the long-term.' Social Care demand is the primary driver.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years of reserve depletion signals the council is not living within operating means; this is the path to reserve exhaustion without structural solutions.
findings.figures: £19.7m overspend against £10.0m contingency
findings.quote: The September forecast outturn position for 2025/26 shows a net £19.7m overspend, which exceeds the £10.0m contingency budget available. If this occurs, it will mark the third consecutive year of relying on one-off funding, an approach that is not financially sustainable in the long-term.

findings.headline: West Sussex faces £30m funding loss over three years from Fair Funding Review 2.0
findings.detail: The council's government funding will fall from £230.4m in 2025/26 to £200.2m in 2028/29, driven by a shift in council tax equalisation from 85% to 100%. This structural cut is partly offset by tax base growth but represents a material headwind to service capacity.
findings.matters: A £30m three-year cut is material for a council of this size and signals pressure on reserves and service delivery, particularly when combined with uncontrolled demand pressures.
findings.figures: £30m loss across three years; £230.4m reducing to £200.2m by 2028/29
findings.quote: loss in funding to the County Council of around £30m across the three-year period

findings.headline: West Sussex faces a potential £40m DSG High Needs deficit liability from 2028/29 when Statutory Override expires, contingent on uncertain government support
findings.detail: The government will meet 90% of cumulative High Needs deficits up to end of 2025/26 (reducing West Sussex's liability from £193m to £19.3m). West Sussex forecasts the DSG deficit will reach £413m by March 2028. The council assumes government will provide 90% support for deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, leaving around £40m as local responsibility when the Statutory Override expires on 31 March 2028. However, the council explicitly states this is uncertain and awaits government clarification on the treatment of future deficits.
findings.matters: A £40m funding liability emerging exactly when the Statutory Override ends represents a material balance-sheet risk for lenders assessing the council's long-term financial resilience and capacity to manage deficits
findings.figures: £193m forecasted DSG deficit by end of 2025/26; £220m further increase to £413m by March 2028; £19.3m immediate local responsibility; around £40m residual liability
findings.quote: leaving a residual deficit of around £40m that would remain a local responsibility when the Statutory Override ends on 31st March 2028

findings.headline: Liability Benchmark shows council will need to maintain external borrowing above £800m through to 2031 to fund capital plans and service the DSG deficit
findings.detail: The council's Liability Benchmark (the minimum debt it could hold if all available cash were used for borrowing) rises from £582.4m in 2026/27 to £906.9m by 2030/31. This is not a forecast of what might happen; it is a constraint showing the level of borrowing the council expects to carry as a matter of necessity. The forecast includes cashflow borrowing for DSG from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: This shows the council is on a committed path to significantly higher debt levels regardless of other choices. The trajectory is structural, not cyclical. A lender needs to understand this is the base case, not a worst case.
findings.figures: Liability Benchmark: £582.4m (31 March 2027), £703.1m (31 March 2028), £850.9m (31 March 2030), £906.9m (31 March 2031)
findings.quote: As set out in Table 7, a forecast of the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit reserve balance has been included in forward looking projections...The Liability Benchmark does however show cashflow borrowing starting from 2027/28 and continuing until a solution in managing the County Council's historic DSG deficit is announced.

findings.headline: Council reduces money market fund investment limit from £200m to £175m, signalling tighter liquidity and planning to divest existing pooled funds
findings.detail: The council is cutting its short-term cash investment limit to reflect lower available cash balances in 2026/27. It is also restricting new long-term investments and considering divestment from existing property and multi-asset funds to generate cash for external borrowing. This signals a real squeeze on available liquidity.
findings.matters: A shrinking investment base and plans to sell long-term holdings suggest the council is running down cash reserves to fund borrowing, not because it wants to but because it has to.
findings.figures: MMF limit reduced from £200m to £175m; maximum long-term investments (greater than one year) limit set at £45m (down from higher historical levels)
findings.quote: A reduction in the total monetary limit from £200m to £175m relating to surplus cash balances being held in sterling liquidity funds (Money Market Funds). This change is recommended to reflect lower cash balances being available for investment in 2026/27

findings.headline: Interest payable rising to £23.3m in 2026/27 as external borrowing increases, with capital financing charges forecast to reach 5.5% of net revenue by 2030/31
findings.detail: New external borrowing in 2026/27 will cost £7.1m in interest on top of £17.6m for existing PWLB debt, totalling £23.3m. This is significant because it marks the start of the transition away from low-cost internal borrowing. The revenue impact shows capital financing charges climbing from 3.8% of net revenue in 2025/26 to 5.5% by 2030/31, reflecting the growing debt burden.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce the council's revenue flexibility and constrain headroom for service pressures or unexpected costs. At 5.5% of revenue, debt servicing becomes a material budget headwind.
findings.figures: Interest payable 2026/27: £23.3m (existing PWLB £17.6m + new borrowing £7.1m); capital financing charges as % of revenue: 3.8% (2025/26) rising to 5.5% (2030/31)

findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to reach £413.9m by March 2028, consuming £241.3m of cash balances and £8.3m of investment income in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The unfunded schools shortfall is growing rapidly (£193.2m in March 2026, £289.2m in March 2027, £413.9m by March 2028) and is held as an unusable reserve under statutory override. The council expects government to take this on from April 2028, but that resolution is still unconfirmed. Until then, the deficit ties up cash and forces borrowing decisions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is betting on government resolution of a £413m liability that currently sits on its balance sheet. If that resolution doesn't come, the council will need either fresh borrowing or material service cuts to generate the cash.
findings.figures: DSG deficit: £193.2m (31 March 2026), £289.2m (31 March 2027), £413.9m (31 March 2028); loss of average cash balances £241.3m in 2026/27; loss of investment income £8.3m in 2026/27
findings.quote: The DSG deficit is currently subject to a MHCLG statutory override that allows the County Council to hold the deficit balance as an unusable reserve to the end of March 2028, therefore not impacting the Council's General Fund. Funding from 1 April 2028 will then be transferred and managed from within central government budgets

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit forces switch from internal to external borrowing strategy after 15 years
findings.detail: West Sussex has used internal borrowing (drawing on reserves and cash balances) since 2010, but a growing DSG deficit leaves insufficient cash. The council forecast external borrowing requirement of £58.5m in 2026/27, with total external debt rising from £437.2m to £677.5m by March 2027. This is the first year of a fundamental shift in finance strategy driven by an unfunded schools funding shortfall.
findings.matters: Switching from internal to external borrowing increases interest costs, reduces financial flexibility, and signals the council's cash position is no longer sufficient to cover capital needs from reserves alone.
findings.figures: External borrowing rising from £437.2m (31 March 2026) to £677.5m (31 March 2027); new borrowing requirement £58.5m in 2026/27
findings.quote: In December 2010, County Council took a decision to introduce an internal borrowing strategy whereby the Council's capital borrowing need is not fully funded by external debt...a switch from an internal to an external borrowing strategy will be required in 2026/27.

findings.headline: £15m uncommitted commitment to speculative Joint Venture development partnership
findings.detail: The Council has up to £15m available for loans to a Joint Venture (Kinsted LLP) for development of surplus land held by the Council. Timing and draw-down are uncertain and depend on planning consent and individual site business cases. Additional funding may be required from either partner if viability issues emerge.
findings.matters: A contingent capital commitment to a speculative property development partnership introduces execution risk and potential for additional funding calls. The timing and quantum are uncertain; returns depend on market and planning outcomes outside the Council's control.
findings.figures: Up to £15m; loans limited to £15m per third party at any one time; Initial capital commitment is land value as a loan
findings.quote: The Capital Programme provides funding of up to £15m towards the County Council's commitment to the Joint Venture as set out in the Partnership Agreement. The exact timing and amount of the actual draw down required will be impacted by the time taken to reach planning consent and the completion of the business cases for each site.

findings.headline: Investment properties generating losses of £0.682m annually despite £18.73m invested
findings.detail: The Council's investment property portfolio, totalling £18.73m in gross book value, is losing £0.682m annually after accounting for £1.262m in capital financing costs against £0.58m forecast income. This represents a negative return and calls into question the investment viability.
findings.matters: A lender examines whether non-treasury investments are generating adequate returns to justify capital deployment and debt financing. Persistent losses on a material portfolio indicate capital allocation risk.
findings.figures: Investment to date: £18.730m; Capital financing costs: £1.262m; Forecast income: £0.580m; Net contribution: -£0.682m
findings.quote: Investment properties 18.730 1.262 0.580 -0.682

findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising to 5.5% of net revenue by 2030/31
findings.detail: The revenue burden of capital programme borrowing (MRP and interest) climbs from 4.4% of net revenue expenditure in 2026/27 to 5.5% by 2030/31. This represents an absolute increase from £38.8m to £57.4m annually in financing charges alone, alongside rising net revenue expenditure.
findings.matters: Escalating debt service as a share of revenue narrows fiscal headroom and indicates tightening affordability. At 5.5% by 2030/31, this is material within a local authority budget.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £38.8m financing costs (4.4%); 2030/31: £57.4m (5.5%); net revenue expenditure 2026/27 £882.9m rising to £1,052.9m in 2030/31

findings.headline: Cash reserves for internal borrowing exhausted from 2027/28 due to DSG deficit
findings.detail: The Council's accumulated DSG deficit will consume all available cash reserves from 2027/28 onwards, eliminating internal borrowing capacity. This forces the Council into external borrowing for capital needs from that point forward, with no relief until a Government funding solution is agreed. The statutory override protecting the Council's balance sheet expires March 2028.
findings.matters: A lender assesses debt capacity and refinancing risk. Loss of internal borrowing reserves materially constrains financial flexibility and increases reliance on external credit markets from 2027/28.
findings.figures: £437.2m existing PWLB debt as of 31 March 2026; DSG Deficit Management Plan shows full cash reserve utilisation from 2027/28
findings.quote: From 2027/28 therefore, no cash reserve for internal borrowing is available until such time that a funding solution for the ongoing DSG deficit is agreed.

findings.headline: Investment cover ratio declining to 1.2 by 2030/31, leaving minimal margin for underperformance
findings.detail: Investment income is forecast to cover borrowing costs at a ratio of 1.0 (2024/25), peaking at 1.6 (2027/28), then declining to 1.2 (2030/31). A cover ratio below 1.25 is below best practice; it means if commercial property or renewable energy returns fall short by just 20%, the council cannot cover debt service from income and must draw on general revenue.
findings.matters: The council's commercial investments (property and Your Energy Sussex renewable schemes) are not fully covering their own financing costs. This creates a revenue drain if returns disappoint. The council is effectively subsidizing these investments from taxpayers.
findings.quote: Investment Cover Ratio 1.0 1.1 1.2 1.6 1.4 1.3 1.2

findings.headline: Internal borrowing reserves will be fully depleted by 2027/28, forcing dependence on external credit
findings.detail: The council's underborrowing position (using internal cash reserves instead of external debt) falls from 19.2% of CFR in 2025/26 to 4.4% in 2026/27, reaching zero from 2027/28 onwards. After that point, every pound of capital financing must come from external borrowing; the council has no liquidity buffer.
findings.matters: Loss of internal borrowing capacity removes the council's ability to manage short-term borrowing needs or adjust strategy if credit markets tighten. A lender must assume the council will need external funding even for ordinary working capital.
findings.quote: Under/Over(-) Borrowing as a % of CFR 11.8% 19.2% 4.4% 0.0% 0.0% 0.0% 0.0%

findings.headline: Debt servicing costs rising to 5.5% of revenue budget by 2030/31, reducing fiscal flexibility
findings.detail: The ratio of Capital Financing Costs to Net Revenue Expenditure is forecast to grow from 3.8% (2025/26) to 5.5% (2030/31). This means an increasing share of the council's revenue is consumed by debt repayment, leaving less for services and reserve building.
findings.matters: A lender cares about what fraction of a council's revenue is tied up in debt service. As this ratio rises, the council's ability to absorb shocks or invest in service improvement declines. 5.5% is entering the zone where it constrains financial management.

findings.headline: Economic development borrowing forecast to nearly double, from £82m to £158m over six years
findings.detail: Capital Financing Requirement specifically for economic developments is forecast to grow from £82.3m (2024/25) to £158.3m (2030/31), with acceleration from 2027/28 onwards. This is new borrowing separate from core service borrowing and includes schemes like Your Energy Sussex (renewable energy and battery storage). The council is taking on significant investment risk on top of its existing debt programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this borrowing will generate returns or create risk. Rapid expansion of speculative lending — and the council tracking it separately suggests it knows it is different from service provision — is a warning sign of overambition.

findings.headline: Commercial investment cover ratio tightening from 1.6 to 1.2 by 2030/31
findings.detail: The investment cover ratio on commercial investments (which includes investment property and Your Energy Sussex schemes) peaks at 1.6 in 2027/28, then declines to 1.2 by 2030/31. This narrow and declining margin means forecasted income barely exceeds the cost of borrowing to fund these investments, with little buffer.
findings.matters: Narrow investment cover ratios indicate commercial schemes are marginal; any income shortfall or rate rise creates vulnerability, and a ratio of 1.2 leaves minimal headroom for risk.
findings.quote: Investment Cover Ratio 1.0 1.1 1.2 1.6 1.4 1.3 1.2; Cost of Borrowing (Capital Financing) 2,591 2,688 2,777 2,907 3,688 4,622 5,316

findings.detail: West Sussex is currently under-borrowing (using internal reserves instead of external debt) to the tune of £77.4m (11.8% of CFR, March 2025). The under-borrowing position increases to £129.9m in 2025/26 but then collapses: by 2026/27 it is only £30.8m (4.4%), and reaches zero by 2027/28. From 2027/28 onward, the council will have exhausted internal resources and must borrow externally.
findings.matters: Depletion of internal borrowing capacity forces the council to rely entirely on external debt markets from 2027/28 onward, reducing financial resilience and increasing refinancing dependence.

findings.headline: New 'Economic Developments' capital financing requirement growing from £82.3m to £158.3m
findings.detail: A distinct capital financing requirement for economic development has emerged, separate from service capital. It grows from £82.3m actual (March 2025) to £158.3m by 2030/31. This appears to be self-contained borrowing for investment property and Your Energy Sussex schemes (battery storage, solar farms, solar panels).
findings.matters: Economic development borrowing is a distinct risk category with its own income-generation and refinancing profile; a near-doubling in five years suggests ambitious economic strategy with reliance on commercial returns.
