findings.headline: Gross external debt projected to grow 60% from £468.5m to £748.7m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's external borrowing is forecast to increase from £468.5m (actual March 2025) to £748.7m by 2030/31. A significant jump occurs between 2026/27 (£497.9m) and 2027/28 (£600.7m), a step change of £103m in one year.
findings.matters: Rapid external debt growth amplifies refinancing risk and increases the council's vulnerability to rising interest rates; a 60% increase in five years is material.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising from 4.1% to 5.5% of net revenue expenditure
findings.detail: The percentage of the council's revenue budget consumed by capital financing costs is forecast to increase by 1.4 percentage points over six years. While 5.5% is not extreme, the upward trend indicates that more of the revenue budget will be locked into servicing past capital decisions, reducing flexibility for service delivery.
findings.matters: Rising capital financing ratios constrain the council's financial flexibility and limit headroom for unexpected pressures or service changes.
findings.figures: Ratio 4.1% (2024/25 actual) rising to 5.5% (2030/31); absolute costs rising from £31,715k to £57,441k

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 47% over five years, from £655.7m to £960.6m
findings.detail: The council is committing to a substantial capital programme that will require £960.6m of funding by 2030/31, compared to £655.7m in March 2025. This represents significant growth in the debt burden the council must service. The growth accelerates in the medium term, with a £130m jump between 2026/27 and 2027/28 alone.
findings.matters: A 47% increase in the capital financing requirement over five years signals either ambitious capital ambitions or deferred commitments now coming due, both material to debt serviceability.
findings.quote: Capital Financing Requirement (Closing Balance) 655,717 677,773 708,388 788,911 857,136 915,912 960,613

findings.headline: Highways and Transport programme, the largest capital portfolio, is forecast to overspend by £4.821m
findings.detail: Highways and Transport, representing the largest single capital programme at £50.106m, is currently forecast to spend £54.927m by year-end, an overspend of £4.821m or 9.6%. Actuals to September are £26.425m with £28.502m remaining in-flight forecast.
findings.matters: Overruns in the largest capital portfolio have material impact on total capital spending and may require budget reallocation or additional borrowing
findings.figures: 25/26 revised budget £50,106k, full year forecast £54,927k, variance over £4,821k
findings.quote: Highways and Transport

findings.headline: Environment and Climate Change capital programme has expanded to £13.887m, three times the revised budget of £4.614m
findings.detail: The Environment and Climate Change portfolio, originally budgeted at £2.259m and revised to £4.614m including acceleration from prior year, is now forecast to cost £13.887m. This £9.273m variance represents a 200% overspend against the revised budget, with £10.258m of remaining in-flight commitments.
findings.matters: A mid-year capital expansion of this magnitude suggests unplanned scope creep or reprioritization; it represents a material unfunded capital commitment that will require funding solutions
findings.figures: Original 25/26 £2,259k, revised £4,614k, full year forecast £13,887k, variance over £9,273k
findings.quote: Environment and Climate Change

findings.headline: Highways and Transport portfolio shows £4.8m overspend on the council's largest capital programme area
findings.detail: This service represents 45% of total capital budget. With revised budget of £50.1m forecast to reach £54.9m (9.6% overspend), and £26.4m already spent at September, sustained cost pressures are evident throughout the forecast period.
findings.matters: Persistent overspend on the largest capital portfolio indicates systematic underestimation of transport infrastructure costs with implications for multi-year capital planning and borrowing
findings.figures: Revised Programme £50,106k; Full Year Forecast £54,927k; Variance £4,821k; Actuals to date £26,425k

findings.headline: Environment and Climate Change portfolio surges to £13.9m (£9.3m overspend) from £4.6m revised budget
findings.detail: The largest single variance on the monitor represents a 201% increase from approved budget. The £2.4m slippage acceleration from 2024/25 accounts for part of the surge, but over £5m is forecast for remaining periods, indicating substantial new commitments in this area mid-year.
findings.matters: A three-fold escalation in environmental spending mid-year represents a major unplanned capital commitment with significant debt servicing and financial resilience implications
findings.figures: Revised Programme £4,614k; Full Year Forecast £13,887k; Variance £9,273k; Slippage/(Acceleration) £2,355k

findings.headline: Capital programme forecasted to overspend revised budget by £18.5m across most service areas
findings.detail: The total revised capital programme is £111.2m but full year forecast is £129.7m. This £18.5m overspend is spread across seven of eight service portfolios, with particular pressures in Highways (£4.8m), Environment (£9.3m), and Children's services (£2.7m), indicating systematic cost pressures or mid-year scope changes.
findings.matters: Widespread capital overspends indicate the council may have underestimated project costs or taken on additional capital commitments, requiring either reserve drawdown or additional borrowing
findings.figures: Total Revised Programme £111,217k; Full Year Forecast £129,682k; Variance £18,465k

findings.headline: Waste contracts expiry triggers procurement risk and expected cost inflation of £75k
findings.detail: The council's waste contracts are expiring and flagged as a growth item of £75k, indicating that contract renewal is expected to drive cost increases. This is a procurement-triggered pressure with ongoing implications.
findings.matters: Waste procurement is a major cost; contract expiry creates budget uncertainty and the council has already identified cost increase risk
findings.quote: Waste Contracts expiry and future procurement strategy Growth 75

findings.headline: Water bills are increasing by approximately 45% to unit costs, creating £120k pressure
findings.detail: The council notes water bills rising c.45% on unit costs, creating £120k pressure. This is an external cost driver outside the council's control and a concrete example of utility inflation compounding budget pressures.
findings.matters: Utility cost inflation of this scale affects multiple budget lines and demonstrates external cost drivers councils cannot control; a 45% increase is significant
findings.figures: c.45% increase to unit costs; £120k pressure
findings.quote: Increased water bills (c.45% increase to unit costs) Pressure 120

findings.headline: Highways maintenance pressure of £3m indicates deferred maintenance or asset deterioration now requiring investment
findings.detail: Additional highways maintenance of £3m is listed as growth. This suggests either a backlog of deferred maintenance becoming urgent or accelerated deterioration of the road network (from age, climate, or heavy use).
findings.matters: Large highways maintenance pressures indicate aging asset base and capital expenditure requirements; this affects long-term financial resilience and suggests previous underinvestment
findings.quote: Additional Highways Maintenance Growth 3,000

findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs are under £7.4m pressure, the largest item in children's services
findings.detail: Support for children placement costs (fostering, residential, supported accommodation) faces £7.4m of pressure. This is 70% of the children's services total pressures and reflects both rising numbers of children needing care and higher provider fees.
findings.matters: Placement costs are statutory and cannot be deferred; rising pressures indicate either worsening child protection caseloads or market-driven provider fees, both of which signal stress in the system
findings.quote: Support for Children (excluding Disabilities) - placement costs Pressure 7,400

findings.headline: SEND home-to-school transport demand pressure of £1.9m shows rising numbers of pupils requiring support
findings.detail: SEND home-to-school transport is under £1.9m pressure from demand growth. This is separate from assessment capacity and indicates both rising SEND identification and potentially longer or more complex routes.
findings.matters: SEND transport is a statutory obligation that cannot be deferred; persistent growth limits financial flexibility and suggests worsening needs profile
findings.quote: SEND Home to School Transport - demand for pupils with SEND Pressure 1,900

findings.headline: SEND assessment backlog required £450k one-off investment to clear; ongoing provision now costs £750k annually
findings.detail: The Special Educational Needs Assessment Team was under-resourced and behind on assessments. The council committed one-off funding in 2024/25 to clear the backlog, and now faces a permanent £750k annual cost to maintain current delivery levels. This indicates systemic under-funding.
findings.matters: SEND assessment delays create legal risk and parental disputes; under-resourcing suggests a service under chronic strain that will not improve without sustained additional investment
findings.quote: Education Health and Care Needs Assessments - short term additional SENAT staffing requirement in 2024/25 (£450k) to meet backlog. Pressure 225

findings.headline: Population-driven adult services demand growth of £3.1m reflects demographic change and rising complexity
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies £3.1m of demand growth from population increase, plus £1.3m from transitions from children's services and £3m from rising complexity of needs. These are structural, not temporary, and total £7.4m of pure demand growth in adult services.
findings.matters: Demographic pressures are persistent; they will not reduce without service model changes and create an ongoing baseline increase to budget requirements
findings.figures: Demand growth due to population increase 3,100; Transitions from Children's 1,300; Rising complexity of needs 3,000
findings.quote: Demand growth due to population increase Growth 3,100

findings.headline: Adult Services market sustainability pressure of £6.3m indicates rising care provider costs and market stress
findings.detail: Market sustainability pressure is the largest single pressure item in the budget. This is coded language for what councils pay care homes and domiciliary providers—they are demanding higher fees. This pressure will recur and is not a one-off.
findings.matters: Rising care provider costs indicate a structural challenge to adult services funding and signal potential market instability that could affect service continuity
findings.quote: Market Sustainability Pressure 6,300

findings.headline: £1.5m loss realised on Federated Hermes property fund redemption
findings.detail: The Interest Smoothing Account is absorbing a £1.5m realised loss on redemption from the Federated Hermes Property pooled fund due to merger with L&G. This is a direct cash loss that reduces available reserves to cover the budget gap.
findings.matters: Investment losses reduce cash available to offset budget deficits and signal either adverse pooled fund performance or governance issues in treasury management.
findings.figures: Property fund loss: £1,500k; Interest Smoothing Account variation: £1,500k
findings.quote: Forecast £1.5m realised loss on redemption from Federated Hermes Property pooled fund on merger with L&G property fund (open only to Pension Funds)

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves depleting by £29.8m to absorb budget pressures
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves projected to fall from £142.8m to £123m between September 2025 and March 2026. Major planned drawdowns include Waste Materials Resource Management (£13m), Digital Infrastructure (£1.5m), and Highways Commuted Sums (£1.6m). The council is applying these reserves to both planned capital and recurring service commitments.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion to cover recurring pressures is structurally unsustainable and signals either permanent budget deficits or deferred capital liabilities that have come due.
findings.figures: Earmarked Reserves Sept 2025: £142,803k; Projected March 2026: £123,037k; Planned reduction: £29,791k
findings.quote: TOTAL EARMARKED RESERVES -152,828 -142,803 -123,037 29,791

findings.headline: Employer National Insurance Contributions grant £3.1m below budget
findings.detail: Council budgeted £3m for NI Contributions grant but now forecasts a shortfall of £3.109m for the full year. This is part of a £4.833m total financing shortfall that is unmatched by any contingency or additional income allocation.
findings.matters: A £3.1m unplanned grant reduction is a significant funding gap that compounds pressure to cover the £19.7m net overspend and increases reliance on reserves.
findings.figures: NI Contributions Grant: budgeted £3,000k, forecast shortfall £3,109k; Total Financing variation £4,833k
findings.quote: Employer National Insurance Contributions Grant -3,000 -3,000 -3,055 -3,109

findings.headline: £4.5m doubtful debts provision signals material income collection deterioration
findings.detail: Non-portfolio budget shows an unplanned £4.5m allowance for doubtful debtors, indicating a material increase in expected uncollectable debts. This sits alongside a £1.108m collection fund deficit and £616k business rates shortfall, totalling £5.7m of unplanned income gaps.
findings.matters: Deteriorating debt collection and revised income assumptions signal cash flow risk and reduce funding predictability—core concerns for lenders assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Doubtful Debtors £4,500k; Collection Fund Deficit £1,108k; Business Rates shortfall £616k
findings.quote: Allowance for Doubtful Debtors 0 0 0 4,500

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care driving £22.76m of spending overruns
findings.detail: Adults Services forecasts £12m overspend and Children, Young People and Learning forecasts £10.76m overspend against approved budgets. These two portfolios account for the bulk of the council's £24.49m total portfolio spending variance and represent structural pressures in demand-led services.
findings.matters: Social care cost pressures exceeding budget allocations by 4-5% suggest demographic demand, unit cost inflation, or service changes not reflected in financial planning—all material to revenue sustainability.
findings.figures: Adults Services variation £12,000k; Children, Young People and Learning variation £10,760k; combined £22,760k of £24,490k total portfolio overspend
findings.quote: Adults Services 292,017 292,159 163,364 12,000; Children, Young People and Learning 236,204 237,141 156,116 10,760

findings.headline: Multiple savings totalling £3m+ depend on delivery of transformation programmes with no published milestones or contingency plan.
findings.detail: Early Support Programme (£1m), Children's Home Collaborative Phases 1&2, and non-statutory and statutory service transformation all have savings contingent on successful delivery of ongoing transformation initiatives. No completion dates or contingency if transformation delays are mentioned.
findings.matters: Portfolio of savings is at risk if transformation programmes do not deliver to schedule; a lender would want to know whether there is a fallback plan.
findings.figures: £1m (Early Support), £1m (Connected Council Transport), plus unquantified transformation savings
findings.quote: Through service remodelling and the Council's transformation programme, it has believed that alternative provision can be made for existing customers which will deliver better value for money.

findings.headline: Prevention and Reablement savings of £1m depend on doubling the demand reduction rate from the prior year, with mechanism unclear.
findings.detail: In 2025/26, reablement growth delivered £1m demand reduction. The proposal targets £2m demand reduction for 2026/27 (doubling the rate) to realise £1m saving, for cumulative benefit of £3m. The council does not explain how further reablement capacity growth will achieve accelerated demand reduction, or what happens if demand does not fall as planned.
findings.matters: A material saving depends on specific demand trajectory; if reablement demand does not fall as planned, this £1m saving will not materialise.
findings.figures: £1m achieved 2025/26; £2m target 2026/27; £3m cumulative; £1m saving value
findings.quote: Growth in reablement capacity was agreed over a two year period in 2025/26 and 2026/27. The benefit of the new contract enabled a £1m reduction in demand growth for 2025/26. A further reduction of £1m is already planned for 2026/27. This proposal will increase that target to £2m and the cumulative benefit to £3m.

findings.headline: The largest single Adults Services saving (£1.4m) depends on unspecified 'practice changes' to absorb means-tested contribution risk.
findings.detail: The council proposes to 'absorb the risk included under pressures by implementing practice changes' but gives no detail on what those changes are or how they will be implemented. This is vague language for a material and material saving.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what practice changes are driving this saving and how certain their delivery is; vague proposals suggest delivery risk.
findings.quote: Proposal is to absorb the risk included under pressures by implementing practice changes (1,400,000)

findings.headline: Adult social care facility closures carry redundancy cost uncertainty; up to £976k of potential costs are flagged but net outcome is unclear.
findings.detail: New Tyne (15-bed closure) assumes £516k max redundancy costs that will 'reduce through redeployment'. The separate review of council-run learning disability homes does not specify a redundancy cost cap at all. Both closures are contingent on successful redeployment or could require reserve funding.
findings.matters: Adult social care savings assumptions may not materialise if redundancy costs are higher than estimated or redeployment does not happen.
findings.figures: New Tyne: max £516k redundancy against £460k saving; learning disability homes review: £900k saving with unspecified redundancy risk
findings.quote: Potential need to fund redundancy costs. Estimated at a maximum of £516k but expected to reduce through redeployment.

findings.headline: Three million pounds of the savings plan (11% of the total) comes from a one-time drawdown of the Lane Rental Reserve for highways maintenance.
findings.detail: This treats a specialist reserve as general budget funding. The Lane Rental scheme funds are being deployed to cover routine maintenance. If highways maintenance demand continues, the reserve will be depleted without a clear replenishment plan, creating a sustainability issue.
findings.matters: A lender assesses council sustainability; one-time reserves use masks underlying structural pressure and cannot be repeated.
findings.figures: £3,000,000 drawdown; £26,574,000 total savings (11%)
findings.quote: Drawdown from Lane Rental Reserve towards highways maintenance (3,000,000)

findings.headline: Children's Services transition funding is a critical dependency for a £1m saving; without it, costs will shift elsewhere.
findings.detail: The Early Support Programme proposal (£1m saving) requires £1.3m of growth funding to pay for young people transitioning from Children's Services to Adults. The council explicitly warns that without this funding, 'there becomes a cost shunt' and the saving will not be deliverable. The growth funding is not yet confirmed as part of the budget.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know whether £1m of the £26.6m total is at material risk of not delivering, and whether the cost will reappear elsewhere in the budget.
findings.figures: £1.3m growth required; £1m saving contingent on it
findings.quote: £1.3m will need to be funded as growth for young people who will transition from Children's to Adults. Without that, there becomes a cost shunt and so the transitions element of the saving will not be deliverable.

findings.headline: Service pressures of £33.6m for 2026/27 are driven by demand growth in adult social care (£17.1m) and children's services (£10.7m)
findings.detail: The council faces £33.6m in service pressures for 2026/27, with nearly 83% of this driven by demand and cost growth in adult social care (£17.1m) and children's services (£10.7m). These pressures are described as presenting 'significant challenges' and the sustainability of local government finances is dependent on managing them through national reform or substantial funding injection.
findings.matters: Demand-driven pressures in social care are structural and difficult to control; they indicate an underlying demographic and legislative burden that will continue to grow regardless of council efficiency, reducing financial flexibility and sustainability.
findings.figures: Total service pressures £33.6m; Adult Services £17.1m; Children and Young People £10.7m
findings.quote: Ongoing pressures, particularly within social care and Special Education Needs and Disabilities (SEND) budgets continue to present significant challenges and the sustainability of local government finances will be dependent on managing these areas either through national reform or a substantial injection of funding.

findings.headline: Transformation savings of only £4.6m are ready for 2026/27; most savings delayed until 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The council has identified only £4.6m in transformation savings for delivery in 2026/27, with the majority of the full savings from transformation programmes expected in 2027/28 and beyond. This means the council is relying on cost reductions that have not yet been implemented to meet its budget target.
findings.matters: Relying on undelivered transformation savings creates execution risk; if these programmes slip or underdeliver, the council's budget gap will worsen with no alternative mitigation identified.
findings.figures: £4.6m transformation savings in 2026/27; full savings 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: While transformation activities will take some time to deliver and the full saving opportunities will be 2027/28 onwards, £4.6m of savings have been identified for delivery in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit remains major concern; Government's SEND reform financing plan not expected until December 2025
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is explicitly flagged as 'a major concern for the County Council' and details on the Government's plan for financing SEND reform are awaited, with publication expected in mid-December 2025. This represents an unquantified liability that could materially impact the council's finances once clarified.
findings.matters: An unresolved liability of unknown size is a significant financial risk; the timing (post-budget setting) means the council may not be able to fully factor this into 2026/27 planning, creating a contingency exposure.
findings.figures: SEND reform financing details expected mid-December 2025
findings.quote: Additionally, the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit remains a major concern for the County Council and further details on the Government's plan for financing SEND reform are now expected in December.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap reaches £72m over five years (2026/27 to 2030/31) even with maximum council tax increases
findings.detail: Even after the £26.6m of proposed budget reductions for 2026/27, the cumulative budget shortfall grows to £72.2m by 2030/31. This indicates a structural, worsening financial position across the medium term that cannot be resolved by reductions in a single year.
findings.matters: The growing cumulative gap shows the council's financial trajectory is deteriorating; this indicates pressures that are structural and demand-driven rather than cyclical, and suggests the council may face difficult choices about service sustainability.
findings.figures: Cumulative shortfall of £72.2m by 2030/31; year-by-year gaps: 2026/27 £16.3m, 2027/28 £25.1m (cumulative £41.4m), 2028/29 £22.4m (cumulative £63.8m), 2029/30 £1.2m (cumulative £65.0m), 2030/31 £7.2m (cumulative £72.2m)
findings.quote: For 2026/27 to 2030/31, as shown in table 4, there remains a budget shortfall of £72m assuming a 4.99% Council Tax increase.

findings.headline: Current year (2025/26) budget is already overspending by £17.6m, driven by adult social care and SEND
findings.detail: In Q1 2025/26, the council reported an overspend of £17.6m against a balanced budget that was only set in February 2025. The overspend is concentrated in Adult Social Care, Children's Services and SEND, indicating that demand pressures are growing faster than anticipated and the underlying cost drivers are not being controlled.
findings.matters: A council already overspending significantly in the current year signals that budget pressures are structural and accelerating, not one-off; this reduces confidence in the ability to meet 2026/27 targets.
findings.figures: £17.6m overspend in Q1 2025/26; concentrated in Adult Social Care, Children's Services and SEND
findings.quote: It showed an overspend of £17.6m, mainly on Adult Social Care, Children's Services and SEND.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 will reduce West Sussex funding by £10m in 2026/27, with £30m loss over three years
findings.detail: The council's early modelling indicates a potential loss of funding of circa £30m across the 3-year period as a result of Fair Funding Review 2.0 reforms. Of this, £10m is estimated to fall in 2026/27, with £10m for each of the subsequent two years. This is a key driver of the budget gap.
findings.matters: A material, quantified loss of government funding in the medium term is a significant structural pressure that reduces the council's financial flexibility and increases reliance on council tax or service cuts.
findings.figures: £10m loss in 2026/27; £30m loss over 3 years; transition arrangements not yet confirmed
findings.quote: For West Sussex, these challenges have been further exacerbated with the expected outcomes of the Fair Funding Review (FFR) 2.0 where our estimated loss in funding is £10m.

findings.headline: Budget shortfall of £16.3m for 2026/27 remains unmet after maximum cost reductions and council tax increase
findings.detail: Despite identifying £26.6m of budget reductions and assuming a 4.99% council tax increase, West Sussex faces a remaining gap of £16.3m for the 2026/27 budget. This shortfall exists even with the maximum available council tax increase and represents the difference between total expenditure of £899.4m and total funding of only £856.5m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can balance its budget and operate sustainably; an unmet gap of this scale after maximum available measures raises questions about the council's ability to manage its financial position.
findings.figures: £16.3m shortfall; total expenditure £899.4m; total funding £856.5m; council tax increase of 4.99%
findings.quote: Financial plans show a budget shortfall of £16.3m for 2026/27, assuming the maximum 5% increase in Council Tax.

findings.headline: ICB restructuring forces 50% cost reduction by December 2025; risk of unfunded function transfers to council without agreed governance or resources.
findings.detail: The register identifies a live risk from NHS England abolition and ICB restructuring: 'ICB's will be required to reduce their operational/staffing costs by 50% and do so by Dec 2025.' Sussex and Surrey ICBs are merging. The council risks having 'current ICB functions not considered to be core to strategic commissioning will be transferred to the council without agreement, governance (e.g. legislation, timing) or additional financial/operational resource.' A mapping exercise of organisational engagement with NHS Sussex was to be completed by December 2025.
findings.matters: Forced transfers of unfunded health-related functions at short notice would create immediate budget pressure and disrupt service delivery. This is a live risk with a December 2025 deadline that may affect the council's financial position mid-cycle.
findings.figures: ICB cost reduction deadline: December 2025; mapping exercise completion deadline: December 2025
findings.quote: ICB's will be required to reduce their operational/staffing costs by 50% and do so by Dec 2025. If ICB's in Sussex and Surrey merge to develop plans in line with the Model ICB Blueprint without collaborating significantly with the council to consider the impact on specific pressures, commitments and priorities (e.g. devolution submission, SEND, safeguarding), there is a risk that current ICB functions not considered to be core to strategic commissioning will be transferred to the council without agreement, governance (e.g. legislation, timing) or additional financial/operational resource.

findings.headline: Water neutrality requirements have halted all council projects in Sussex North Water Supply Zone, blocking school expansion and capital investment.
findings.detail: A Natural England position statement from September 2021 'has essentially halted all WSCC plans and projects in the water supply zone until water neutrality can be demonstrated.' The principal identified risk is the council's inability 'to provide sufficient school places in the water neutrality area.' A local authority-led offsetting scheme is planned for spring 2025 launch, but this remains an active constraint on capital deployment and service expansion in a significant part of the county.
findings.matters: A major council unable to expand school capacity in part of its territory is a service delivery and demographic pressure point. Capital constraint reduces flexibility to respond to growth or change.
findings.figures: £250,000 secured from Planning Skills Delivery Fund (December 2023) to support offsetting scheme; offsetting scheme planned launch spring 2025
findings.quote: Natural England issued a Position Statement on 14 September 2021 that affects all planning applications not granted before that date within the Sussex North Water Supply Zone. This has essentially halted all WSCC plans and projects in the water supply zone until water neutrality can be demonstrated.

findings.headline: Adult social care provider market in acute stress: 14 services closed or handed back contracts in 12 months; 16 high-risk contracts remain.
findings.detail: The register reports 14 adult social care provider closures or contract handbacks in the last 12 months and identifies 16 high-risk contracts requiring increased monitoring. The council cannot fully fund provider fee increases: 'adult social care budget position limits the ability to increase fees in line with budget pressures felt by providers from economic and legislative changes.' Care assistants can no longer be recruited directly from abroad and current overseas workers face uncertain status changes in 2028 when visa transition ends, threatening staffing stability.
findings.matters: Repeated provider exits reduce service resilience and increase council's own cost exposure. Fee pressure unable to match provider costs creates ongoing market instability risk and potential service gaps requiring emergency provision or council investment.
findings.figures: 14 services closed/handed back in 12 months; 16 high-risk contracts identified in Q1 2025/26; overseas care worker visa transition period ends 2028
findings.quote: In the last 12 months 14 services in West Sussex have closed and or handed back contracts. The position continues to be reviewed and reported regularly.

findings.headline: The council faces a structural funding gap with no Government solution to the DSG deficit and growing social care pressures.
findings.detail: The register identifies lack of new central government funding combined with inflation, interest rates, and rising pressures in social care, home-to-school transport and SEND. Critically, there is 'No solution from Government on the statutory over rides relating to pooled investments and the DSG deficit ending in 2025/26, with responsibility for any financial implications falling to the County Council.' The council is using reserves annually to balance budgets, with a note that 'Any use of reserves to balance the budget are assumed to be replenished.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budget gaps are being managed through planned savings or through one-off reserve drawdowns. This shows structural pressure with no visible funding solution from Government.
findings.figures: 2026/27 MTFS update published July 2025; budget prep for 2026/27 started April 2025
findings.quote: The financial sustainability of council services is at risk due to the lack of new funding from central government, the impact of economic conditions (mainly inflation and interest rates) and the growing services pressures, particularly around social care, home to school transport and SEND.

findings.headline: NHS partnership pooled budget arrangements remain unresolved with deadline of 31 March 2026 and proposal to merge two ICBs creates further uncertainty
findings.detail: The council and NHS Sussex have agreed to review their current pooled budget agreements, which cover a range of social care and NHS services. A new arrangement must be reached by 31 March 2026 at the latest, but 'a new arrangement has yet to be agreed.' Additionally, a proposal to merge NHS Sussex and NHS Surrey ICBs is due to be considered by NHS England later in 2025, which would require the council to reconsider the governance and commissioning implications with East Sussex and Brighton and Hove councils.
findings.matters: Unresolved partnership arrangements nine months out create planning uncertainty; ICB merger proposal adds further structural uncertainty to health-social care commissioning and could affect budget assumptions
findings.figures: Deadline 31 March 2026; ICB merger decision expected 2025
findings.quote: The Chief Executives of the Council and NHS Sussex have agreed to progress a review of the current pooled budget agreements between the Sussex ICB and the council. Discussions are continuing between the County Council and the ICB. Although a new arrangement has yet to be agreed, both partners remain committed to the process and intend for change to be made by 31 March 2026 at the latest.

findings.headline: Finance team workforce planning strategy to be developed, suggesting current capacity and succession planning concerns
findings.detail: The council has identified the need to develop a dedicated Workforce Planning Strategy for Finance, including review of balance of resources and grades, succession planning, and career progression opportunities. This is scheduled for March 2026 completion and reflects concerns about finance team capacity and capability to support budget management and transformation.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity constraints affect the council's ability to deliver financial controls, budget management, and transformation programmes; succession planning gaps create continuity risk for CFO-level oversight
findings.figures: Strategy due March 2026
findings.quote: Develop a Workforce Planning Strategy for Finance - including consideration of: a. Balance of resources and grades reflecting the level of work within the Strategic Finance teams b. Succession planning c. Career grades for trainees

findings.headline: Oracle Fusion financial system implementation has auditor concerns and HR/Payroll modules remain off-schedule for April 2026
findings.detail: The council is replacing its core SAP financial system with Oracle Fusion. Finance and Procurement modules are due end-2025. HR and Payroll modules are due April 2026. External auditors have raised ongoing concerns about the implementation as a VFM issue and noted the council's recovery actions since the programme restarted. Scrutiny committee receives regular monitoring reports.
findings.matters: Large system implementations carry delivery and control risk; auditor concerns signal the council does not consider the implementation trajectory low-risk; payroll module delay into April 2026 maintains implementation risk through budget-setting period
findings.figures: Finance/Procurement go-live end-2025; HR/Payroll April 2026
findings.quote: External Auditor – generally positive VFM conclusion for 2023/24 except for ongoing concerns with the Oracle implementation project (with narrative included in Auditor's Annual Report), although there was recognition of the positive actions that had been taken place since the programme restarted.

findings.headline: Teachers' Pension regulatory breach identified in 2021; individuals are now being notified of options with backdated contribution liability
findings.detail: The council notified the Pensions Regulator in June 2021 of a breach involving the failure to auto-enrol some part-time and casual teaching staff into the Teachers' Pension Scheme following a 2007 regulation change. From April 2025, affected individuals are receiving options papers and will face decisions on scheme participation with backdated contribution obligations.
findings.matters: A confirmed regulatory breach affecting scheme members creates potential liability for backdated contributions and ongoing administrative/compliance costs; shows governance failure spanning multiple years before discovery
findings.figures: Breach notification June 2021; individuals notified April 2025 onwards
findings.quote: In June 2021 the Council notified the Pensions Regulator of a breach of the Teachers' Pension Regulations. This related to a failure over a number of years to auto-enrol some part time and casual teaching staff onto the teachers' pension scheme as required following a change to the regulations in 2007.

findings.headline: Recruitment and retention remains a high corporate risk, particularly in adult and children's social care
findings.detail: The council identifies recruitment and retention as a high-risk item on its Corporate Risk Register. Specific service areas—adults' and children's social care—have faced persistent recruitment and retention challenges. An internal audit review of strategic workforce planning concluded with limited assurance, and the council is developing a workforce planning strategy.
findings.matters: Persistent recruitment and retention failure in social care undermines service quality and consistency; limited assurance from audit on workforce planning suggests systemic planning weakness
findings.figures: Recruitment and retention flagged as high-risk; 6 of 32 internal audit reviews (19%) concluded in limited assurance
findings.quote: Recruitment and Retention remains a high risk on the Corporate Risk Register and updates are regularly reported to the Performance and Finance Scrutiny Committee. Management actions are being progressed following a limited assurance result from an internal audit review on strategic workforce planning.

findings.headline: DSG statutory override expires March 2026 and the council is lobbying government for a long-term solution
findings.detail: The statutory override that has allowed the council to manage deficits on the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) is due to end in March 2026. This end-date is now nine months away and the council has not secured a long-term government solution, creating a time-bound cliff-edge risk to the budget.
findings.matters: A significant protection expires in nine months; if no solution emerges, the council will absorb an undefined DSG deficit into its general budget
findings.figures: DSG override ends March 2026; specific deficit amount unspecified
findings.quote: The statutory override to manage the deficit balance on the DSG currently ends in March 2026 and the County Council continues to lobby Government for a long-term solution.

findings.headline: MTFS identifies a funding gap in future years requiring savings plans alongside pressure management
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy explicitly identifies a funding gap in forward years. The council faces pressures in demand (especially adult and children's social care) and must develop savings plans to bridge the gap, with particular uncertainty around government policy changes including devolution and local government reorganisation.
findings.matters: An identified funding gap signals the council faces structural deficit risk beyond the current year and has not yet quantified how it will close the gap
findings.figures: Funding gap identified but amount unspecified; MTFS covers five years
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) identifies a funding gap in future years. Pressures and Growth need to be managed alongside savings plans that should consider the longer term.

findings.headline: 2024/25 overspend funded by reserves is not sustainable and prompts enhanced monitoring
findings.detail: The council overspent in 2024/25 and covered the deficit using reserves. Leadership acknowledges this is not sustainable and has put additional reporting arrangements in place, with enhanced monthly updates to executive leadership on Adults and Children's services, which are the areas facing the greatest financial risk.
findings.matters: A council funding its operating deficit through reserves is by definition unsustainable and indicates deteriorating budget control in the largest service areas
findings.figures: 2024/25 overspend (amount not specified); covered by reserves
findings.quote: The Council overspent in 2024/25 which was funded through use of reserves. This is not sustainable and so additional reporting arrangements have been put in place.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Annual Governance Statement Action Plan 2024/25
findings.headline: A pooled budget agreement with the Sussex Integrated Care Board is in dissolution, with renegotiation ongoing to March 2026.
findings.detail: The council and Sussex ICB are working to end their current pooled budget arrangement by 31 March 2026. This affects how integrated care services (likely adults' health and social care) are financed and governed going forward, and renegotiation has already carried over from 2023/24.
findings.matters: Pooled budgets are material financial arrangements; their dissolution signals a change in service delivery structure and financial accountability that affects the council's integrated care partnership.
findings.figures: Deadline 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Work is continuing with the ICB about the dissolution of the pooled budget agreement.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Annual Governance Statement Action Plan 2024/25
findings.headline: A Teachers' Pension enrolment issue affecting 134 employees remains unresolved after four years.
findings.detail: West Sussex has a historic enrolment issue with the Teachers' Pension Scheme affecting 134 current and former employees, ongoing since 2021/22 with March 2026 deadline. The scheme has completed calculations for 92 individuals, 15 have responded with the majority choosing to purchase backdated service—a cost the council may need to fund.
findings.matters: This is a multi-year contingent liability with financial implications; the scale (134 people, calculations for 92) and the backdated service purchases represent potential balance-sheet obligations a lender would scrutinise.
findings.figures: 134 current and former employees; 92 individuals with contribution and interest calculations completed; 15 responded to options letter
findings.quote: The County Council continues to work closely with the Teachers' Pension Scheme to resolve a historic enrolment issue affecting 134 current and former employees, including those employed by organisations for whom West Sussex previously provided payroll services.

findings.headline: Cannot fully assure Property, Plant & Equipment and Reserves balances due to disclaimed opinions on 2022/23; gap will not be closed in 2024/25
findings.detail: Because the auditor disclaimed opinions on 2022/23 and 2023/24, they lack assurance over opening balances for Property, Plant & Equipment and Reserves for 2024/25. The auditor states: 'we do not have assurance over the completeness and accuracy of movements in 2022/23, and as a result lack assurance over the full population of PPE and associated transactions.' This limitation will continue into 2025/26.
findings.matters: PPE and Reserves are major balance sheet categories. Without full audit assurance, there is material uncertainty about the asset base and financial reserves available to manage risk or fund operations.
findings.figures: Affects PPE and Reserves balances; gap will take several years to close under NAO's Local Audit Reset and Recovery Implementation Guidance
findings.quote: we do not have assurance over the completeness and accuracy of movements in 2022/23, and as a result lack assurance over the full population of PPE and associated transactions

findings.headline: Oracle Fusion IT programme commits council to £26 million over 2024/25–2027/28, in addition to £13 million already spent
findings.detail: The council is proceeding with a replacement Enterprise Resource Planning system (Oracle Fusion) after terminating the previous SmartCore contract in September 2023. The May 2024 decision commits the council to £26 million additional funding, covering external support, programme delivery team, and £4 million contingency. The auditor notes the programme was previously flagged as a significant value-for-money weakness and had governance issues, but these have been mitigated.
findings.matters: A £26 million IT investment represents a material capital commitment and operational risk. The project's history of problems and cost escalation (£13m already spent on a cancelled project) demonstrates execution risk that could affect service delivery and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £26 million 2024/25–2027/28; £13 million previously spent; go-live planned January and April 2026
findings.quote: This new name reflects the name of the Council's preferred solution but also demarcating a fresh start to the project. The decision to progress with this project was made in May 2024 and commits the Council to funding of up to £26 million over the period 2024/25 to 2027/28, in addition to the £13 million spent under the SmartCore project.

findings.headline: PFI accounting errors: £15.158 million amendment made, with unadjusted £5.283 million understatement remaining in opening liability
findings.detail: The council's application of IFRS 16 to three PFI schemes (Street Lighting, Recycling & Waste, Crawley Schools) contained errors in inflation indexation. The council amended the accounts by £15.158 million, but the auditor identified a net understatement of £5.283 million in the opening liability (Crawley Schools understated by £8.983 million; Street Lighting overstated by £3.7 million). The auditor and council's models differ due to indexation treatment.
findings.matters: PFI liabilities are long-term fixed obligations. Accounting errors here affect the reliability of the balance sheet and the council's ability to service debt. The council is also recommending it revisit modelling for 2025/26.
findings.figures: £15.158 million amendment; £5.283 million unadjusted net understatement
findings.quote: We compared the Councils revised models to our own modelling and note a total net understatement in the opening liability at 1 April 2024 of £5.283m. This is due to differences in the application of indexation for inflation to elements of the unitary charge within the Crawley Schools and Street Lighting PFI.

findings.headline: £16.187 million correction to pension liability due to asset ceiling calculation error in IAS 19 reporting
findings.detail: The council's actuary's IAS 19 reports did not include the impact of interest cost relating to the 31 March 2024 asset ceiling. This required a £16.187 million adjustment to the pension reserve. The error affected the Movement In Reserves Statement, Cash Flow Statement, Expenditure & Funding Analysis, and five notes to the accounts.
findings.matters: A £16m error in pension liability is material and indicates control weaknesses in the finance function's review of pension accounting. Pension liabilities are a major balance sheet item for councils.
findings.figures: £16.187 million adjustment
findings.quote: We identified a £16.187 million adjustment to the Councils IAS 19 pension balances, as the IAS 19 reports used to prepare the draft financial statements and did not include the impact of the interest cost relating to 31 March 2024 asset ceiling.

findings.headline: Audit opinion remains uncertain; council received disclaimers on 2022/23 and 2023/24, and 2024/25 opinion not yet finalised
findings.detail: The council cannot obtain a clean audit opinion on prior years. The auditor states: 'we have not yet obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances.' The council is considering whether to issue a qualified opinion for 2024/25 instead of a disclaimer. This means the financial statements lack full audit assurance.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on audited accounts to judge financial health. An unclean opinion means the accounts are unreliable as a basis for lending decisions.
findings.figures: Backstop date for 2024/25 audit: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: we have not yet obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances

findings.headline: Loss of schools SLA income of £239k due to academisation represents structural income reduction
findings.detail: The council is experiencing a permanent loss of schools service level agreement income as schools transition to academy status. This £239k reduction is marked as an ongoing pressure for 2025/26, indicating continued academisation is eroding the council's income base.
findings.matters: Academisation reduces the council's controllable income base structurally and permanently; this is not a cyclical pressure but an ongoing erosion of revenue.
findings.quote: Loss of Schools SLA Income due to Academisation Pressure 239

findings.headline: Water bills are facing approximately 45% increase in unit costs, a major cost inflation shock
findings.detail: The council faces increased water bills with a 45% increase to unit costs, quantified as a £120k pressure. This represents a significant cost inflation shock beyond the council's control affecting all operations.
findings.matters: A 45% cost increase is substantial and unavoidable; it indicates the council faces material cost pressures from utility inflation that cannot be managed through service change.
findings.figures: c.45% increase to unit costs; £120k quantified pressure
findings.quote: Increased water bills (c.45% increase to unit costs) Pressure 120

findings.headline: Housing Related Support costs of £520k are currently funded on a temporary basis by the Public Health Grant
findings.detail: The council is meeting housing related support costs through temporary Public Health Grant funding. The document explicitly marks this as a temporary arrangement, creating uncertainty about funding from 2026/27 onward.
findings.matters: Temporary funding arrangements indicate future budget risk; loss of this funding would require the council to either find alternative funding or reduce this service.
findings.quote: Housing Related Support costs temporarily funded by Public Health Grant Pressure 520

findings.headline: SEND-related spending pressures total at least £2.9m, reflecting growing demand
findings.detail: The council faces home to school transport demand pressure of £1.9m, Special Educational Needs Assessment Team ongoing pressure of £750k, and Educational Psychology Service pressure of £264k. These are all marked as ongoing 2025/26 pressures and are demand-driven.
findings.matters: SEND demand is growing faster than councils can control; these pressures indicate the council is under significant strain in this area and may require sustained additional funding.
findings.figures: SEND Home to School Transport £1,900k; SENAT ongoing 2025/26 £750k; Educational Psychology Service £264k
findings.quote: SEND Home to School Transport - demand for pupils with SEND Pressure 1,900

findings.headline: Adult Services market sustainability pressure of £6.3m is the single largest identified pressure
findings.detail: The council faces a market sustainability pressure of £6.3m in Adult Services alongside demand growth of £3.1m, rising complexity of needs at £3m, and transitions from children's services at £1.3m. These four factors alone total £13.7m in Adult Services pressures.
findings.matters: Market sustainability pressure in social care is a known risk area for councils; a £6.3m single-line pressure indicates material budget stress if unaddressed.
findings.figures: Market Sustainability £6,300k; Demand growth £3,100k; Rising complexity £3,000k; Transitions from Children's £1,300k
findings.quote: Market Sustainability Pressure 6,300

findings.headline: West Sussex has identified £33.6m in quantified service spending pressures for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council has documented known spending pressures totaling £33,638k across all services for 2025/26. The largest concentrations are in Adult Services (£17.1m) and Children, Young People and Learning (£10.7m). This represents the scale of budget challenge the council faces beyond baseline spending.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the magnitude of pressures the council faces and whether it has credible plans and funding sources to address them.
findings.figures: Overall total £33,638k; Adult Services £17,120k; Children, Young People and Learning £10,664k; Highways and Transport £3,550k
findings.quote: Overall total 33,638

findings.headline: Finance and Property portfolio cut by £5.4m between February forecast and June revised position
findings.detail: Finance and Property was initially forecasted at £20.2m in February but adjustments of £5.4m were made, reducing it to £14.8m revised budget—a 27% cut within four months. This substantial mid-year reprofiling raises questions about the reliability of earlier forecasts.
findings.matters: Large reprofiling adjustments in either direction within the financial year indicate weak budget forecasting and control, which lenders view as a governance risk.
findings.figures: February programme £20,237k; Adjustments (£5,420k); Revised £14,817k

findings.headline: Highways and Transport, the largest capital portfolio at £50.1m, is overspending by £4.5m
findings.detail: Highways represents the council's single largest capital investment at £50.1m revised budget but is forecast to spend £54.6m—a 9% overspend of £4.5m. As the largest portfolio, this overspend contributes materially to the total programme variance.
findings.matters: Overspend on the largest capital programme suggests schemes are either running over cost or behind schedule, with cost recovery. This is material to financing risk and cash flow planning.
findings.figures: Revised £50,106k; Forecast £54,577k; Variance £4,471k over

findings.headline: Environment and Climate Change portfolio more than doubled from revised budget, adding £8.3m
findings.detail: The Environment portfolio was revised at £4.6m in June but is now forecast to spend £12.9m—an £8.3m increase. This represents an 178% variance and suggests either substantial cost inflation on environmental schemes or major scope additions.
findings.matters: A near-doubling of spending on one portfolio within months of the revised budget indicates loss of budget control, delivery risk, or unplanned commitments that will require explanation and additional funding.
findings.figures: Revised £4,614k; Forecast £12,864k; Variance £8,250k over

findings.headline: Total capital programme forecast to overspend by £15.8m against revised budget
findings.detail: The council's total revised capital programme for 2025/26 is £111.2m, but the full year forecast is £127.0m—an overspend of £15.8m. This represents 14% variance against the revised budget and indicates that capital schemes are running over budget, requiring either additional funding or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Material capital overspend signals delivery risk and raises questions about whether the council can execute its plans within budget or will need additional borrowing to finance the overrun.
findings.figures: Revised £111,217k; Forecast £127,022k; Variance £15,805k over budget

findings.headline: Support Services and Local Government Reorganisation shows £10.7m budget with zero planned spend for the year
findings.detail: This portfolio was budgeted at £11.95m, reprofiled down by £1.25m to £10.7m, but shows zero actuals to date and zero forecast for the remaining period, meaning the entire £10.7m is unscheduled.
findings.matters: A fully-allocated but entirely unscheduled capital budget suggests either a stalled project or funds held pending approval; either way, it affects the timing of borrowing needs and the credibility of the capital plan
findings.figures: £10,700k revised budget, £0 actual spend, £0 forecast
findings.quote: Support Services and Local Government Reorganisation 11,950 0 11,950 (1,250) 10,700 0 10,700 0 10,700 0

findings.headline: Highways and Transport is forecast to overspend by £4.5m on a £50.1m budget
findings.detail: The highway capital program was held flat at £50.1m after adjustments but is now forecast to reach £54.6m, representing a £4.5m (8.9%) overspend. Actuals to date show £10.6m spent with £44.0m forecast to come.
findings.matters: Highways typically represents stable, predictable capital spend; an 8.9% overspend signals either inflation in delivery costs or unplanned maintenance needs that will require additional borrowing
findings.figures: £50,106k programme, £54,577k forecast, £4,471k variance

findings.headline: Environment and Climate Change capital program has jumped to £12.9m, nearly 9 times the original budget
findings.detail: The in-flight program was £2.3m, adjusted to £4.6m mid-year, but is now forecast at £12.9m for the full year. The £8.25m variance represents 366% of the original budget, suggesting either a major new commitment or significant repricing of an existing scheme.
findings.matters: A three-fold increase in capital plans mid-year, especially in a discretionary area like climate change, indicates changing priorities or unanticipated scope that will require additional borrowing
findings.figures: £2,259k original, £4,614k adjusted, £12,864k forecast, £8,250k variance

findings.headline: Total capital program is forecast to overspend by £15.8m, a 14% variance on the revised budget
findings.detail: The revised capital program for 2025/26 is £111.2m after mid-year adjustments, but the full-year forecast is £127.0m. This means the council is now projecting it will spend £15.8m more than the revised budget across all portfolios.
findings.matters: Capital overspends affect the council's borrowing requirement and available headroom; a 14% variance at portfolio level signals either scope creep or cost inflation that will increase external borrowing
findings.figures: £111,217k revised, £127,022k forecast, £15,805k variance

findings.headline: Inflation assumption at 2.5% CPI exposes budget to shortfall given actual June 2025 inflation of 3.6% and macro risks
findings.detail: Current working inflation envelope is 2.5% CPI, but actual inflation in June 2025 stood at 3.6%. The paper acknowledges 'the outlook for inflation is particularly difficult to forecast' due to global trade tariffs, Middle East crisis, and Ukraine conflict. Assumptions will be reviewed following September CPI data and OBR Autumn Statement forecasts.
findings.matters: The 1.1 percentage point gap between assumption and current reality represents material unbudgeted exposure; external macro risks are acknowledged but cannot be controlled
findings.figures: June 2025 CPI: 3.6% actual; 2.5% working assumption
findings.quote: Price inflation (CPI) remains above the Bank of England's target of 2% with June 2025 at 3.6%. However, changes in global trade tariffs, the Middle East crisis and Ukraine conflict, mean the outlook for inflation is particularly difficult to forecast

findings.headline: Pay award uncertainty: annual awards confirmed post-budget approval on a £320m pay bill with 1% award costing £3.2m
findings.detail: National and local pay agreements are 'invariably confirmed post the annual budget approval,' creating forecast risk. The council employs 5,982 FTE excluding schools. A 1% pay award costs approximately £3.2m. The paper assumes 3% annual growth from 2026/27 onwards but this is assumption, not committed.
findings.matters: Pay is the council's largest cost element; annual uncertainty in pay inflation on a £320m budget, compounded by uncertain future assumptions, creates budget control and cash flow risk
findings.figures: £320m pay budget 2025/26; 5,982 FTE; £3.2m per 1% award; 3% assumed growth from 2026/27
findings.quote: Annual pay awards are determined by national and local agreement which are invariably confirmed post the annual budget approval

findings.headline: Waste sector faces £1m-£2m net cost from Deposit Return Scheme and up to £7m annual cost from Emissions Trading Scheme from 2028
findings.detail: The Deposit Return Scheme (October 2027) will reduce recyclates but also reduce income from sale of materials, creating a net £1m-£2m pressure. From 2028, if Emissions Trading Scheme is applied to energy-from-waste, costs could reach £7m per annum at £80/tonne. The council is lobbying against the producer-pays principle shift but cannot control the outcome.
findings.matters: These are large quantified future pressures; the ETS risk alone amounts to material annual expenditure that is outside the council's control
findings.figures: £1m-£2m net pressure (DRS from October 2027); up to £7m annually (ETS from 2028 at £80/tonne)
findings.quote: It is expected that this will be a net pressure (£1m-£2m) although this will be driven by customer behaviour and the impact on recycling levels. At present this cost would fall to the council, with estimates that this could be up to £7m (£80 per tonne)

findings.headline: Highways infrastructure needs extended capital investment beyond the £10m already allocated for 2025/26
findings.detail: Changing rainfall patterns have increased flooding events. The 2025/26 budget includes an additional £5m revenue and £10m capital for proactive maintenance and drain capacity. However, the paper states 'to maintain the highways network and reduce the backlog of works in the medium term may require further capital and revenue investment.'
findings.matters: This represents both ongoing capital pressures and the risk of an expanding infrastructure backlog; climate-driven flooding is structural rather than cyclical
findings.figures: £5m additional revenue 2025/26; £10m additional capital 2025/26
findings.quote: To maintain the highways network and reduce the backlog of works in the medium term may require further capital and revenue investment

findings.headline: Home to School Transport costs rising annually due to EHCNP numbers and staffing costs, with statutory obligations limiting options
findings.detail: West Sussex has a statutory duty under the Children and Families Act to provide transport for pupils with Education Health and Care Needs Plans. The number of EHCNPs is rising, and staff costs (particularly for escorts) are increasing, driving annual cost growth that the council cannot discretionarily avoid.
findings.matters: This is a statutory obligation with demographic drivers; cost growth cannot be managed through discretionary service changes and will continue to compound
findings.figures: No specific figures provided, but annual growth is ongoing
findings.quote: Due to rising numbers of EHCNPs and the impact of staff costs, and in particular escorts, Home to School transport cost is increasing annually

findings.headline: Adult social care cost growth set to accelerate due to wage pressures and market constraints
findings.detail: The council faces simultaneous cost drivers in adult social care: a government ban on overseas care workers coupled with 'fair pay agreements' to improve employment terms; National Living Wage rising 3.6% (projected £12.65/hour for April 2026); and unfunded increases in employer National Insurance contributions. The paper explicitly states 'it is highly likely that the price of care is set to increase significantly in real terms.' The council is a minority purchaser in a buoyant self-funder market, limiting its negotiating power.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically a council's largest budget; accelerating care costs in a tight market can rapidly erode financial sustainability and constrain other services
findings.figures: 3.6% projected National Living Wage growth (central estimate £12.65/hour); £320m total council pay budget; care market minority purchaser position
findings.quote: when added to the impact of the NLW and to the recent unfunded changes to the cost of employer National Insurance contributions, it is highly likely that the price of care is set to increase significantly in real terms

findings.headline: 2024/25 overspend of £10.1m met from reserves drawdown
findings.detail: West Sussex overspent by £10.1m in 2024/25 and covered this through a drawdown from reserves. The paper states many of these pressures are anticipated to continue into 2025/26 and beyond. This signals both past budget control issues and ongoing structural pressures.
findings.matters: A £10.1m reserve hit is material; it reduces financial headroom and the continuation of these pressures into the forward years indicates the problem is unresolved
findings.figures: £10.1m overspend
findings.quote: the County Council faced pressures that exceeded the budget provision resulting in an overspend of £10.1m, which was met from a drawdown from reserves

news_drafts.headline: Allowance for doubtful debts increased significantly to £17.7m, driven by legacy adult social care contributions
news_drafts.lead: A large doubtful debt provision is both an immediate hit to resources and a signal of underlying income collection problems. The link to social care assessments and COVID-19 legacy suggests structural delays in the council's processes.
news_drafts.paper_title: Annex B - Performance and Resources Report – Q4 2025/26

news_drafts.headline: 39% of planned savings were not delivered in 2025/26 and are being pushed into 2026/27
news_drafts.lead: Inability to deliver planned savings, especially in the year they are due, indicates either operational challenges or optimistic planning. Pushing these into the next year while new pressures continue to emerge raises the risk of compounding deficits.
news_drafts.paper_title: Annex B - Performance and Resources Report – Q4 2025/26

news_drafts.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown to £202.995m and represents the largest structural fiscal risk
news_drafts.lead: A £203m deficit is a material contingent liability that affects the council's balance sheet and borrowing capacity. The grant cover is not guaranteed—approval of the SEND plan is a condition precedent. If not approved, the council's liability explodes.
